Vectors and arithmetic

Imagine you work for a small retail company. You have the prices and quantities sold for 5 products:

prices     <- c(12.5, 8.0, 23.99, 5.50, 15.0)
quantities <- c(3, 10, 1, 25, 7)

  • Compute the total revenue across all products: use sum(prices * quantities).

  • How many products are there? Use length(prices).

  • What’s the most expensive product? Use max(prices).

  • What’s the cheapest? Use min(prices).

  • What is prices[3]? What is prices[c(1, 4)]?

  • Use seq() to create a vector of discount percentages from 5% to 50% in steps of 5%.

Missing values and help

You have monthly sales data, but two months are missing:

monthly_sales <- c(120, 95, NA, 210, NA, 180)

  • Try mean(monthly_sales). What happens?

  • Use ?mean to find the argument that ignores missing values. Compute the mean without NAs.

  • How many values are missing? Use is.na() and sum().

  • Use ?max. Compute the maximum sale ignoring NAs.

  • Run ?seq. What does the length.out argument do? Use it to create a vector of 7 evenly spaced values between 0 and 1.

Data frames

Build a data frame from the vectors you created in Exercise 1:

products <- data.frame(
  name     = c("Pen", "Notebook", "Backpack", "Eraser", "Marker"),
  price    = prices,
  quantity = quantities
)
  • Use dim(products). How many rows and columns?
  • Use colnames(products) and str(products) to inspect the data frame.
  • Access the price column with products$price.
  • Access the 3rd row with products[3, ].
  • What element is in row 2, column 3?
  • Use summary(products). What’s the average price?
  • Show only products with quantity > 5: use products[products$quantity > 5, ].

Fix the code

Each code snippet below contains a mistake. Copy it, run it, read the error message, then fix it.

my_vec <- c(1, 2, 3
maen(my_vec)
My_Vec
matrix(1:6, nrow = 2, ncol = 4)

Logical values and comparisons

You recorded daily temperatures for a week:

temps <- c(18, 22, 25, 30, 28, 35, 20)
  • Which days were above 25°C? Use temps > 25. What type of object is the result?
  • How many days were above 25°C? Use sum() on the logical vector.
  • Use which(temps > 25) to get the positions of the hot days.
  • Which days were between 20 and 30 (inclusive)? Combine conditions with &: temps >= 20 & temps <= 30.
  • Were there any days below 15 or above 34? Use |.

Factors

A survey records education levels:

edu <- c("high school", "bachelor", "master", "bachelor", "high school", "PhD", "master")
  • Convert edu to a factor with as.factor(edu). How does it print differently from the original vector?
  • Use levels() and nlevels() to inspect the factor.
  • Now create an ordered factor with factor(), specifying levels = c("high school", "bachelor", "master", "PhD") and ordered = TRUE.
  • Run sort() on the original character vector and on the ordered factor. What is the difference?
  • Use table(edu) to count how many respondents fall in each category.

Sequences and repetitions

  • Use seq(0, 1, by = 0.1) to create a vector from 0 to 1 in steps of 0.1. How many elements does it have?
  • Use seq(0, 100, length.out = 5) to create exactly 5 evenly spaced values between 0 and 100.
  • Use rep("A", times = 4) to repeat "A" four times.
  • Use rep(c("A", "B"), times = 3) and rep(c("A", "B"), each = 3). What is the difference?
  • Combine: create a vector with the numbers 1 to 3 repeated 4 times each, followed by the value 99. Use c(), rep(), and a scalar.

Matrices

Build a 3x4 matrix of the numbers 1 to 12:

m <- matrix(1:12, nrow = 3, ncol = 4)
  • Print m. Does R fill the matrix by columns or by rows?
  • Use nrow(m), ncol(m), and dim(m).
  • Extract the element in row 2, column 3. Extract the entire second row. Extract the entire fourth column.
  • Use colSums(m) and rowSums(m). Verify one result by hand.
  • Try matrix(1:12, nrow = 3, ncol = 4, byrow = TRUE). What changes?

Lists

Create a list that stores information about a student:

student <- list(
  name   = "Alice",
  grades = c(28, 30, 25, 27),
  passed = TRUE
)
  • Print student. How does it differ from a vector?
  • Access the name with student$name and with student[["name"]].
  • Compute the average grade: mean(student$grades).
  • Use names(student) and length(student).
  • Add a new element: student$university <- "Milano". Print the list again.

Putting it all together

Build a small dataset about 5 cities:

cities <- data.frame(
  name       = c("Milan", "Rome", "Naples", "Turin", "Bologna"),
  population = c(1396000, 2873000, 967000, 886000, 395000),
  north      = c(TRUE, FALSE, FALSE, TRUE, TRUE)
)
  • Inspect the data frame with str() and summary().
  • Show only northern cities: cities[cities$north == TRUE, ].
  • Add a new column density that equals population / 100 (a made-up simplification). Use cities$density <- ....
  • Which city has the highest population? Use which.max(cities$population) to get its row index, then extract the city name.
  • Sort the data frame by population in decreasing order: cities[order(cities$population, decreasing = TRUE), ].

Practice 2: Visualisation with txhousing

The txhousing dataset is included in the tidyverse. Load it with:

library(tidyverse)

Then type txhousing to see it. It contains monthly housing sales data for 46 Texas cities (2000–2015).

  • Exercise 1
  • Exercise 2
  • Exercise 3
  • Exercise 4
  • Exercise 5
  • Exercise 6
  • Exercise 7
  • Exercise 8
  • Exercise 9
  • Exercise 10

Explore the data

  • Run head(txhousing) and str(txhousing).
  • How many observations are there? Use dim().
  • Run summary(txhousing). What is the range of median house prices? Are there missing values?
  • Compute the average median house price with mean(). Remember na.rm!

Your first scatterplot

  1. Build a scatterplot of sales (y-axis) vs listings (x-axis):
ggplot(data = txhousing, aes(x = listings, y = sales)) +
  geom_point()

  1. Add labels with labs():

    • x-axis: "Active listings"
    • y-axis: "Number of sales"
    • title: "Texas housing market"

  2. Apply theme_minimal().

  3. Store the final plot in an object called my_plot.

Distributions

  1. Build a histogram of median (median house price):
ggplot(data = txhousing, aes(x = median)) +
  geom_histogram()

Try bins = 10, bins = 30, and bins = 100. What happens with very few vs very many bins?

  1. Build a bar chart showing how many records there are per year:
ggplot(data = txhousing, aes(x = year)) +
  geom_bar()
  1. Add labs() to both plots.

Comparing across groups

  1. Build a boxplot of median house price by month:
ggplot(data = txhousing, aes(x = factor(month), y = median)) +
  geom_boxplot()

Which month has the highest median prices? The most spread?

  1. Build a boxplot of sales by month. Is there a seasonal pattern?

  2. Use ?geom_boxplot. Can you find an argument to change the fill color of the boxes? Try it!

  3. Add labs() and theme_minimal().

Color and facets

  • Build a scatterplot of volume (y) vs sales (x), colored by year:
ggplot(data = txhousing, aes(x = sales, y = volume, color = year)) +
  geom_point()
  • What trend do you see?
  • Add facet_wrap(~month). Does the pattern change across months?
  • Add labels and a theme.

Numeric vs factor color

  1. Build a scatterplot of listings vs sales, coloring points by month:
ggplot(data = txhousing, aes(x = listings, y = sales, color = month)) +
  geom_point()

What kind of color scale do you get (continuous gradient or discrete palette)?

  1. Now convert month to a factor inside the aes():
ggplot(data = txhousing, aes(x = listings, y = sales, color = factor(month))) +
  geom_point()

How does the legend change? Which version is more informative for this variable?

  1. Add labs(color = "Month") and theme_minimal() to the second version.

Subsetting before plotting

  1. Create a subset of txhousing containing only Houston, Dallas and Austin:
three_cities <- txhousing[txhousing$city %in% c("Houston", "Dallas", "Austin"), ]

  1. How many rows does three_cities have? Use dim().

  2. Build a scatterplot of listings vs sales using three_cities, colored by city:

ggplot(data = three_cities, aes(x = listings, y = sales, color = city)) +
  geom_point()

  1. Add facet_wrap(~city) to separate each city into its own panel. Add labels and a theme.

  2. Try adding San Antonio to the subset and re-run the plot. Does the pattern change?

Creating new variables and plotting

  1. Compute the average price per sale and add it as a new column:
txhousing$price_per_sale <- txhousing$volume / txhousing$sales

  1. Check the result: head(txhousing$price_per_sale). Are there NAs? Why?

  2. Build a histogram of price_per_sale:

ggplot(data = txhousing, aes(x = price_per_sale)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40)

  1. Build a boxplot of price_per_sale by year. Use factor(year) on the x-axis so each year gets its own box. Is the average price per sale increasing over time?

  2. Add appropriate labels and theme_minimal().

Combining logical filters with ggplot

  1. Create a logical vector that identifies summer 2010+ observations:
is_summer_recent <- txhousing$year >= 2010 & txhousing$month %in% c(6, 7, 8)

  1. How many TRUE values are there? Use sum().

  2. Subset the data: summer_recent <- txhousing[is_summer_recent, ].

  3. Build a scatterplot of median (y) vs listings (x), colored by factor(year):

ggplot(data = summer_recent, aes(x = listings, y = median, color = factor(year))) +
  geom_point()
  1. Add facet_wrap(~month) to separate June, July, and August. Add labels and a theme.

Changing color palettes

Start from the scatterplot of Exercise 6 with discrete month colors:

ggplot(data = txhousing, aes(x = listings, y = sales, color = factor(month))) +
  geom_point()

  1. Apply a ready-made palette with scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set3"). Try also "Paired" and "Dark2". Which one do you find most readable?

  2. Now use a manual palette. Define your own vector of 12 colors (one per month) and apply it:

my_colors <- c("Jan" = "#1f77b4", "Feb" = "#ff7f0e", "Mar" = "#2ca02c",
                "Apr" = "#d62728", "May" = "#9467bd", "Jun" = "#8c564b",
                "Jul" = "#e377c2", "Aug" = "#7f7f7f", "Sep" = "#bcbd22",
                "Oct" = "#17becf", "Nov" = "#aec7e8", "Dec" = "#ffbb78")

To use named colors you first need to label the months. Create a labeled factor:

txhousing$month_name <- factor(txhousing$month,
                               levels = 1:12,
                               labels = c("Jan","Feb","Mar","Apr","May","Jun",
                                          "Jul","Aug","Sep","Oct","Nov","Dec"))

Then plot with color = month_name and add scale_color_manual(values = my_colors).

  1. Try the continuous version: plot color = median (a numeric variable) and apply scale_color_gradient(low = "blue", high = "red"). How does it differ from the discrete palettes?

  2. Add labs() and theme_minimal() to your favourite version.
